Class AnswerRule

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.rl.AnswerRule
public final class AnswerRule extends Object
A rule the fighter is held to, like the one about the sword's charge (SwingGate): hit, and not yet having hit back, it swings the moment its sword is back and the game has the opponent under its crosshair within reach. Not left to the network: taking hit after hit with the sword back and a hit there to be made is something it must not do at all, and what it had learned of when to swing back was, some rounds, never.

What it goes by is the fighter's own count of the hits it has taken in a row, and the game's own pick of what is under the crosshair: the thing the attack indicator shows a player, and what a click is decided by. So a swing made by this rule is one that reaches. (The first version went by how tall the opponent stood in the picture. Hit, a fighter is flying backwards, the picture is a tick old, and nearly every one of those swings met air: 98 in 100 of its swings in the air, and each of them cost it the sword for the next exchange.)

The pick is taken twice. Once when the step is decided: if the rule applies, the attack key is not the network's on that tick, as with the rule about the sword's charge. And again when the click is made, after the camera has turned: if the opponent is no longer under the crosshair the swing is not made at all, and the sword stays back.

Made on the tick it learns of the opponent's hit, before the knockback has carried it out of reach, such a swing is what players call a hit-select: a sprint hit takes four tenths off the attacker's own speed, so it is thrown less far than the opponent it has just hit, and the next hit is its own.

  • Method Details

    • inTheAir

      public static int inTheAir(float[] vec)
      When the swing it owes is made, with the opponent under its crosshair. On the ground: now. In the air it is kept for the way down, where it is a critical hit, the punish crit: half as much damage again. A hit throws a fighter up for four or five ticks and it comes down for as many; on the way up the swing is not made, on the first tick of the way down the sprint is let go of (the game makes no critical hit of a sprinting player's swing, and hears of the sprint ending at the end of that tick), and on the next the swing is made.

      Up to the first fights of 0.14.0 against a person the swing was made the moment the rule applied, which in the air is on the way up: a hit, and the sword gone for the fall. The punish crit was then made only where the rule had not applied first, and a player who goes round the fighter making critical hits, each of which leaves it in the air with that player in reach, got plain hits back for them.

    • onTheGround

      public static int onTheGround(float[] vec, boolean punishable)
      When the swing it owes is made while its feet are on the ground. Against most opponents: now, which is a trade, hit for hit. Against one that was still in reach the last time it came down from a hit (FallWatch), it is kept for as long as the hit is fresh (the twenty ticks its clock runs): on the tick of the hit itself, so that it is still there for the way down, where it is a critical hit; and after a fall on which no swing was to be had, until the next hit, which from such an opponent is never long in coming.

      Why not at once there too: an opponent that stays on top of the fighter hits it every fifteen to twenty ticks. A swing made from the ground a moment before that hit is a plain hit or a sweep, and it leaves the sword on its way back for the whole of the next fall. Measured against the opponent that takes no knockback, an hour into the first rules: on 46% of its falls with that opponent in reach the sword was not back, eight of its hits in ten were sweeps, and the share that were critical had gone from three in four to four in ten.

    • onTheGround

      public static int onTheGround(float[] vec, boolean punishable, boolean wait)
      Parameters:
      wait - keep the swing for as long as the hit is fresh, as up to 14 October; false keeps it on the tick of the hit only. With the jump made with a hit (JumpReset) the opponent is in reach on nearly every fall, so it was nearly always "one that stays", and a second after each hit it stood in reach with its sword back and did not swing: what a person saw was a fighter that is close and does not hit.

    • when

      public static int when(float[] vec, boolean punishable, boolean proven)
      When the swing it owes is made, on the ground or in the air; see onTheGround(float[], boolean) and inTheAir(float[]).

      Keeping the swing is for the first hit. Hit a second time in a row without having hit back, it is being comboed, and then the hit that is there is the hit that is made: now, on the ground or on the way up, critical or not. What it is held to first is that no combo goes by without a swing back, and a swing kept for a fall on which the opponent is then out of reach is a combo sat through. (With the swing kept whenever the last fall had the opponent near, one combo in seven went by without a swing, where it had been one in twenty-five.)

      Unless a punish crit has been made on this opponent: the last fall on which the sword was back ended in one (FallWatch.proven). Then the fall is where the next one is made too, second hit or not. (Without that, against the opponents that stay on top of it and make critical hits, a fall with the sword still on its way back was followed by a plain hit made on the way up of the next: three falls in four ending in a critical hit became six in ten.)

      Parameters:
      punishable - the opponent was in reach on the way down the last time
      proven - and a punish crit has been made on it

    • opponentBacking

      public static boolean opponentBacking(float[] vec)
      Whether the opponent is backing straight out after a single hit: in view, its own speed away from the fighter at least BACKING, and not in a combo (the second hit in a row is always answered). That is the spacer's crit, S: the answer then trades at its landing and leaves the sword down for its next jump in, which comes on its own clock (20 October).
